chapters.title: Chapter 2: Computing a Company's Taxable Income

body.text: Your accountant depreciates each asset over the life it is expected to have. The tax law ignores all of that, drops your assets into a handful of buckets, and applies its own percentage to each bucket. Two sets of books, one machine, two different numbers, both correct.

children.text: Depreciation is usually the single largest add-back in a company's computation of income, and the single largest reason its effective tax rate drifts away from 25.17%. A manufacturer that has just built a new line can pay noticeably less tax than its profit and loss account suggests, purely because the tax law lets it write assets down faster than its books do.

body.title: Two systems, running side by side

columns.label: Book depreciation
points: Governed by the Companies Act and accounting standards
Based on each asset's estimated useful life
Straight line or written down value, as the company chooses
Asset by asset, with gain or loss booked on sale
Purpose: show shareholders a fair picture of wear and tear

columns.label: Tax depreciation
points: Governed by section 33 [old 32] and the rules under it
Based on fixed percentages, whatever the asset's real life
Written down value method, with rare exceptions
Block by block, with no gain or loss on an ordinary sale
Purpose: a uniform, dispute-free formula for every taxpayer

markDefs.definition: A group of assets of the same class carrying the same depreciation rate, treated as one pool for tax purposes rather than as individual assets.

children.text: Tax law does not track your lathe and your laptop separately. It puts every asset into a
and depreciates the pool. Buy an asset and its cost joins the pool. Sell one and the money received leaves the pool. Depreciation then applies to whatever is left.

body.caption: The block runs on this one equation, year after year
The main blocks and their rates

cells: Machines, motor cars, equipment, mobile phones
Land never depreciates, however long you hold it

body.text: Notice how rough these buckets are. A precision machine expected to last twenty years and a generator expected to last seven sit in the same 15% block. Your books can reflect the difference. Your tax computation cannot, and is not trying to.

children.text: An asset bought and put to use for less than 180 days in the year gets only half the normal rate that year. The clock runs from the date the asset was actually put to use, not the date on the invoice. A machine delivered in March and commissioned in May earns nothing in the earlier year.

body.label: The cut-off date
body.context: Assets put to use on or before roughly this date get the full rate for the year. Later, and the rate halves. In a year with 365 days, 180 days before 31 March lands in early October.

body.title: A full block computation, worked out

children.text: A Coimbatore engineering company starts the year with a plant and machinery block at a written down value of ₹50,00,000. During the year it buys a machine for ₹20,00,000 in June, another for ₹10,00,000 in January, and sells an old machine for ₹4,00,000.

cells: Used for more than 180 days, so full rate
Sale proceeds leave the block, whatever the book value was
The full-rate portion of the block
Half rate in the first year only
Deducted in the computation of income

children.text: Notice what did not happen. Nobody calculated a profit or loss on the machine that was sold. Its sale proceeds simply reduced the block. From next year, the January machine sits in the pool at the full rate like everything else.

body.title: Try It: One Block, One Year
body.prompt: A company's computer block opens at a written down value of ₹6,00,000. In August it buys laptops worth ₹4,00,000, and it sells no computers during the year. At the 40% rate, what is the depreciation for the year? Answer in ₹ lakh.
body.explanation: The laptops were put to use in August, which is more than 180 days before the year ends, so they earn the full rate. The block is ₹6,00,000 plus ₹4,00,000, which is ₹10,00,000, and 40% of that is ₹4,00,000 or ₹4 lakh. Closing written down value is ₹6,00,000. Had the laptops been bought in February instead, they would have earned only 20% and depreciation would have been ₹2,40,000 plus ₹80,000, or ₹3,20,000.

children.text: Why the Two Numbers Drift, and Then Come Back Together

Take a single machine costing ₹10,00,000. The books write it off evenly over ten years, at ₹1,00,000 a year. The tax computation applies 15% on the reducing balance. In the early years tax depreciation runs well ahead, which is why a company investing heavily in plant pays less tax than its book profit implies.

body.title: Depreciation on a ₹10 lakh machine: books vs tax

children.text: By the end of year five, the books have claimed ₹5,00,000 and the tax computation ₹5,56,295. The gap is real but temporary. Written down value depreciation never quite finishes, while the books stop at ten years, so in later years the position reverses and the company pays more tax than its book profit suggests. Nothing was saved. It was borrowed.

body.text: This is the deferred tax liability on the balance sheet, in plain words. The company has enjoyed a deduction early, owes the difference later, and accounting insists on showing that future obligation now rather than letting shareholders be surprised by it.

body.title: Quick Check: Which Rate Applies?
body.question: A company buys a ₹1,20,000 laptop, a ₹90,000 office cupboard, a ₹8,00,000 delivery van and a ₹5,00,000 patent, all in May. Which one attracts the highest tax depreciation rate?
body.explanation: Computers, including laptops, sit in the 40% block, the fastest write-off in the ordinary rate table. The patent is an intangible at 25%, the delivery van is plant and machinery at 15%, and furniture is at 10%. All four get the full rate here, because they were put to use in May, well before the 180-day cut-off.

children.text: Three Rules Worth Knowing Before You Buy Anything

cells: You cannot skip it to show a higher profit for a lender. The written down value carried forward is reduced as if you had claimed it
Put to use, not merely purchased
An asset lying in a crate earns nothing. Keep installation and commissioning evidence, not just the invoice
Additional depreciation of 20% on new plant and machinery
Available to manufacturers on new, not second-hand, plant and machinery, but given up by any company that has opted into the concessional regime in section 200 [old 115BAA]
If you sell everything in a block, or receive more than its written down value, the excess is taxed as a short-term capital gain

body.title: Scenario: Buy It in March, or Wait for April?
body.scenario: A Pune packaging company plans to buy a ₹60,00,000 machine. Its finance head can place the order so that the machine is commissioned on 20 March, or push it to the second week of April, in the next tax year. The company is profitable, is in the concessional regime under section 200 [old 115BAA], and has no cash constraint either way.
body.prompt: Which timing gives the better tax outcome, and what else should decide this?
body.modelAnswer: Commissioning on 20 March gives only half the rate, because the machine would be in use for fewer than 180 days, so depreciation is 7.5% of ₹60,00,000, or ₹4,50,000, saving about ₹1,13,256 of tax at 25.168% in that year. Waiting until April means no deduction in the current year, but the full 15%, or ₹9,00,000, in the next one, worth about ₹2,26,512. Across two years the April purchase is ahead, and the block then carries a higher written down value into later years as well. So if the choice is purely about tax, April wins. But tax should not decide this alone. If the machine would earn revenue through March, or a supplier discount expires, or a customer order needs capacity now, the commercial gain will usually dwarf the tax difference. The right question is whether the asset can start earning, not which year it lands in. Also note that being in the concessional regime, the company cannot claim the extra 20% additional depreciation on new plant and machinery in either year.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The First-Year Rule
body.textWithBlank: An asset put to use for less than 180 days in the year it is acquired is allowed only ___ of the normal depreciation rate for that year.
body.explanation: Half the normal rate, so 7.5% instead of 15% for plant and machinery, or 20% instead of 40% for computers. The restriction applies only in the first year. From the following year, the asset sits inside the block and earns the full rate like everything else in it.

body.title: What to Keep on File for Every Asset You Buy
steps: The purchase invoice, with GST shown separately, since input tax credit claimed is not part of the asset's cost
Proof of the date the asset was put to use: installation report, commissioning certificate or first production record
Freight, installation and other costs incurred to bring the asset into use, which form part of its cost
The block each asset belongs to, tagged in the fixed asset register at the time of purchase
Sale invoices for assets disposed of, so proceeds reduce the correct block
A note of any asset that is partly used personally, such as a director's car, with the basis of apportionment

cards.definition: The depreciation provision of the Income-tax Act, 2025, operating on blocks of assets at prescribed rates.
A pool of assets of the same class and rate, depreciated together rather than individually.
The opening balance of a block plus additions, less sale proceeds and depreciation already claimed.
An asset put to use for under 180 days in its first year gets half the normal rate that year.
The date the asset actually starts being used for the business, which governs depreciation rather than the invoice date.
An extra 20% of cost on new plant and machinery for manufacturers, surrendered by companies in the concessional regime under section 200 [old 115BAA].
The accounting record of tax postponed because tax depreciation ran ahead of book depreciation.

points: Book depreciation follows each asset's useful life, while tax depreciation under section 33 [old 32] applies fixed rates to blocks of assets
The main rates are 40% for computers, 25% for intangibles, 15% for plant and machinery, 10% for furniture and most buildings, and nil for land
Sale proceeds reduce the block, so an ordinary sale produces no profit or loss in the tax computation
Assets put to use for under 180 days in the first year get half the rate, which makes commissioning dates matter
Depreciation cannot be skipped, and the written down value is reduced as if you had claimed it
The gap between book and tax depreciation is a timing difference, recorded as deferred tax and reversing in later years

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax or accounting advice. Section references reflect the Income-tax Act, 2025 as understood at the time of writing, with the corresponding 1961 Act section shown in brackets. Rates are prescribed by rules and can change, and special rates apply to certain assets and industries not covered here. Consult a qualified chartered accountant before finalising a depreciation claim.
